The published risk of malignancy (ROM) for pulmonary cytopathology cases categorized as “Benign” is highly variable. In most studies, the ROM is between 24% and 42%, and it does not vary to any great extent between the different types of cytopathology specimens {7716347; 26990836; 25640352; 30051969}. A study with stringent criteria for the adequacy of transbronchial FNAB specimens reported a very low ROM of 3% for “Adequate” specimens with a categorization of “Negative”, but the term “Negative” as used in this study differs from the “Benign” category of the WHO Reporting System in that it excludes cases with adequate benign material where the cytopathological finding did not correlate with the imaging findings; it also has to be balanced against a higher “Insufficient” rate in this study {24127207}. In defining adequacy criteria for each type of cytopathological specimen there should be a balance between minimizing the number of “Insufficient” specimens and the risk of a false negative diagnosis {24127207}. Further studies will be valuable for the clarification of the ROM of cases in the “Benign” category.

The “Benign” cytopathology report should be correlated with the clinical and imaging features. The aims of the cytopathology study are to exclude malignancy and to diagnose infections, various inflammatory processes, and benign neoplasms. If the cytopathology report correlates with the clinical and imaging findings, and confirms an inflammatory process or a benign neoplasm, then recommended routine follow-up may be to review the patient in 3–6 months after treatment of any infection, or to get an immediate surgical assessment if the patient has symptoms related to the neoplasm, such as respiratory obstruction.

If a sputum sample “Benign” categorization does not correlate with the clinical and/or imaging findings, then bronchial wash (BW), bronchial brush (BB), and FNAB should be considered for further defining the lesion. Spontaneous or induced sputum sampling can be a first-line test in patients with central nodules or haemoptysis and offers a pooled sensitivity of 66%. Three consecutive samples are recommended, and as many as five samples are suggested, to rule out cancer. Sputum sampling has a relatively high false negative rate because it fails to sample a lesion, which is frequently beneath the bronchial mucosa. If a sputum sample “Benign” report does not correlate with the clinical and/or imaging findings, the patient should be referred to bronchoscopy, where BW and BB can be obtained, especially for central visible lesions. These techniques have a combined sensitivity of 88% {27753244; 8432124}.

The hallmark of granulomatous entities, which can be infectious or non-infectious in etiology, is the presence of necrotizing and non-necrotizing granulomas, with or without necrosis in the background. In the presence of these findings, the cytopathologist or cytotechnologist at rapid onsite evaluation (ROSE) or in the laboratory should determine how to triage the sample for further workup, including special stains, cultures, PCR molecular testing, and sensitivity analysis {30889574}. BW and BB have a low diagnostic yield for detecting granulomatous disease, but BW when combined with sputum sampling has a sensitivity of 88% for detecting acid-fast bacilli. Postbronchoscopy sputum samples can also be collected, with a sensitivity of 35%. Unless the samples are transferred immediately, they should be kept at 0–4 °C.

Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) is the method of choice for the diagnosis of a wide range of interstitial lung diseases, with a sensitivity of 85% (94% when combined with biopsy) {3044685}. If a BW, BB, or BAL “Benign” report does not correlate with the clinical and/or imaging findings, then endobronchial ultrasound or transthoracic FNAB should be considered.

In general, endobronchial ultrasound–guided transbronchial FNAB is best for central submucosal lesions, and transthoracic FNAB is best for peripheral lesions {27753244; 30195266}. CT-directed sampling can be performed for well-defined nodules or non-infectious tumour-like lesions. Benign lesions account for 30% of transthoracic FNAB specimens {26990836}. If an FNAB does not correlate with the clinical and/or imaging findings, transbronchial core needle biopsy should be considered immediately if ROSE has been performed, or at a later procedure. If transbronchial core needle biopsy is not available, consideration should be given for open surgery.

Treatment of benign neoplasms depends on whether the tumour is symptomatic or not, and on the type of tumour. The optimal treatment for endobronchial or symptomatic lesions is limited surgical resection, such as wedge resection, particularly for lesions with reported aggressive potential {18605767}. Otherwise these tumours tend to be slow-growing, with an excellent prognosis, and can be clinically followed up {12232871}.
